articleTitle: Master planning: turning vision into action (change management)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: This paper focuses on the plan for a change programme to create the successful business of the future. To put the need for the plan in context, the authors' surveys and work have led him to conclude that managing directors rightly focus on the long-term vision for the business, but often fail to flesh it out sufficiently to make it tangible to the very managers who have to implement the vision. This is often compounded by failure to communicate the plan, such as it might exist, properly. Middle managers feel they had had a half-thought-through idea dumped on them by a managing director who probably wouldn't be around in two to three years' time when the 'plan' was intended to be delivered. Their questioning is often misinterpreted as resistance. Master planning bridges the gap and turns the long-term vision for the business into practical, tangible plans.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: Whereas much change in manufacturing concentrates on the introduction of new technologies, systems and work methods, this paper focuses on the management and organisational requirements (the 'soft side') necessary to support full exploitation. Examination of research findings from the late 1980s reveals that the problem to be addressed in the 1990s is not that of lack of adoption, but of lack of success in adoption. Variously problems of implementation and inadequate organisational design arrangements necessary to sustain the changes have been blamed for this state of affairs. This paper argues the need for fundamental shifts in the implicit and largely unquestionable assumptions concerning each of these which are contained within the managerial mindset. Collectively these add up to the prevailing organisational culture. A prototyped, field tested tool for driving cultural change by transforming the managerial mindset is outlined.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: MOPS; meeting the needs of UK industry
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: Innovation and continuous improvement are central to the vision that the government has for the future competitiveness of the UK. The difficult economic climate that companies have faced over the last couple of years has provided a great incentive to companies to be innovative in order to survive. As we move out of recession, that impetus for improvement must be maintained by other means. The author details how DTI will continue with programmes that assist industry to take up new ideas, from wherever they come. The best practice that has been identified in programmes such as MOPS (manufacturing operations people and systems) are worth detailed consideration by companies of all types.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: The MOPS initiative recognises that organization and people are an important consideration in manufacturing systems implementation which hitherto was largely ignored. HUMAN CENTRED SYSTEMS Ltd has been involved in developing usable information technology tools to help bridge the gap between manufacturing systems and their users who need information not data. It was a natural extension to these developments that they should get involved in its practical application through Project BESTMAN. Here, the author attempts to explain the work done, and give an indication of the tangible benefits of applying the methodology.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: World class manufacturing culture: an approach developed in the IMOCIM project
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: Any form of improvement requires change. To be successful the change must be appropriate, planned, implemented and monitored. The need for UK manufacturing industry to become more competitive is well documented and is the subject of numerous reports. Here, the author describes the IMOCIM project which has been developed in response to the needs of UK manufacturing which will benefit from a systematic and systemic approach to improving competitiveness.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: In the context of most British industry, North West Water provides an unusual case study of the management of change. The author describes its experience since 1991 of transforming a public utility into an efficient privatised business, which represents major change on many fronts: cultural; financial; organisational; and technological. At the same time, continuity in supplying its traditional public services has been vital.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: The culture at JCB, from its conception, has been epitomised by the Company motto which is 'Jamais Content' and as such, in the 1980s, when times were very good and all-time records were being broken, JCB were still very conscious of its weaknesses and areas it needed to address. Here, the author outlines such a study at JCB, and describes how, as they analysed their current performance, they were aware that teamwork and problem-solving had to be improved and the tremendous latent potential of their staff had to be tapped even further. Initially, their thoughts were to address these two areas of problem-solving and teambuilding with extensive training. However it soon became apparent that these were only a part of an overall quality issue which needed attention.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Destiny-understanding how people really work in manufacturing organisations
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: To be an effective manager you must be able to embrace and control change. People are the key to the effective management of change-how to organise and motivate them, and how they perceive relationships and opportunities. Here, the authors describe Destiny, an approach that uses a diagnostic PC software tool to help managers understand how their companies really work. Destiny thus enhances the prospects for appropriate change, and decreases the chances of implementing costly changes that may not work well.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: The author describes CIGNET, the Continuous Improvement Group NETwork, which is an industry based collaborative research project into current best practice in continuous improvement (CI) initiatives in the North West of the UK. The project is led by NIMTECH The North West Regional Technology Centre who provide programme management and CI expertise. Best practice is researched in the core industrial companies and will contribute towards the generation of methodology and software applications. A group of three local network organisations effectively manage the dissemination of the project findings as well as arranging individual assistance for CI initiatives (embryonic or well established) to regional manufacturing industry.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: The IMOCIM project which received funding support from the Department of Trade and Industry's MOPS initiative began on the 1st of May 1992 and completed on the 31st of October 1993. The objective of this research and development project was to develop a methodology for management of change in manufacturing along with a computer based tool to support the methodology. A basic aim of the methodology to be developed was that a holistic approach to change should be adopted, which embraced people, organisation, systems and technology. This paper describes how the above aims and objectives were achieved together with the results and deliverables available from the project.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Building on our manufacturing base. Attitudes to change in British manufacturing business (management)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: Manufacturing business is news again. The need for a strong manufacturing base is high on the public agenda. But what do we have to build upon? Is manufacturing today lean and mean, or is it suffering from malnutrition? Ingersoll Engineers' annual surveys of manufacturing business give some of the answers. There are grounds for optimism: competitive needs are widely understood, and innovation and hard work are creating more world-class businesses. There are new methodologies to apply, from finance to human factors. Many initiatives are available that should and need not be starved. Above all, in British manufacturing today, the attitude to managing change is the crucial competitive issue.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The introduction of cellular manufacturing at Bomford Turner
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Management of Change
abstract: This paper examines the actions taken by a small company to achieve an advantageous position in a very competitive market. These actions relate to changes in the manufacturing strategy, resulting in a cellular manufacturing implementation that led to a change of culture within a very traditional mechanical engineering environment. The changes were centred around: cellular layout; production and material control system; supplier development; and human resource development. These changes were wrought and substantial gains made with no investment in new plant, no new robotics or CAD/CAM installation, no sophisticated computerized production control system, but with detailed attention being paid to improving the effectiveness of the existing resources, both plant and people. The company, Bomford Turner, is an international supplier of grass hedge cutters and agricultural equipment based at Salford Priors near Evesham, UK.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
